Pregnancy

Ginseng during pregnancy and breastfeeding: is it safe?

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ginseng is promoted for energy, stress and other health concerns, but a long history of use does not establish safety for a developing baby. Avoid starting or continuing a medicinal ginseng product on your own during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Ask your maternity clinician or pharmacist to assess the exact preparation and why you want to use it. If you have already taken some, uncertainty is a reason to seek advice, not proof that harm has occurred.

First identify which ginseng you have

Asian ginseng is Panax ginseng; American ginseng is Panax quinquefolius. Red and white Asian ginseng refer to different processing methods, rather than separate assurances of safety. Products may contain dried root, powder or concentrated extract and come as capsules, tablets, liquids or teas. A product containing several herbs needs an assessment of the whole ingredient list.

Siberian ginseng, Eleutherococcus senticosus, is a different plant. Kew places it and Panax ginseng in the same botanical family, Araliaceae, but in different genera. Evidence for one should not be transferred to the other just because their common names share the word ginseng. Keep the Latin name and product label available when asking for advice.

What do the claimed benefits actually mean?

Claims range from better energy, stress tolerance and immunity to improved blood sugar, memory, sexual function, menopause symptoms, digestion and exercise recovery. These are separate questions: a positive result for one outcome in nonpregnant adults does not establish a benefit for pregnancy fatigue or fetal development.

NCCIH describes much of the research as small and short. Some results suggest modest benefits for general fatigue or erectile function; blood sugar findings are inconsistent, and most research does not show improved athletic performance. Preliminary findings about cognition or influenza do not justify promises to prevent dementia, treat a cold, repair muscle injury or broadly strengthen immunity. Claims about menopause and digestion also should not be presented as established pregnancy benefits.

Antioxidant activity is not a cancer-prevention claim

An antioxidant effect in a laboratory does not show that taking ginseng prevents cancer or heart disease in people. The National Cancer Institute explains that human trials of antioxidant supplements have not established an overall cancer-prevention benefit, and some tested supplements caused harm in particular groups. Those trials are not proof that ginseng itself causes those harms; they show why the word antioxidant cannot establish a clinical benefit.

Do not use a ginseng product as a substitute for cancer treatment or other prescribed care. Any proposed supplement during cancer treatment needs discussion with the treating team.

Why pregnancy guidance is cautious

The European Medicines Agency does not recommend its assessed Panax root medicines during pregnancy or breastfeeding because adequate data are lacking. Its traditional fatigue indication rests on longstanding use rather than sufficient clinical-trial evidence. Health Canada requires advice before use in pregnancy or breastfeeding for products covered by its Panax ginseng monograph. Neither position establishes a pregnancy-safe dose.

The practical advice is to avoid self-treatment and have the product reviewed. This applies throughout pregnancy; a warning that emphasizes early development does not establish that use becomes safe after the first trimester. Safety findings from healthy adults using ginseng for a short time cannot answer the pregnancy question.

What the embryo studies can and cannot tell us

A 2003 experiment exposed cultured rat embryos directly to an isolated ginseng constituent, ginsenoside Rb1. Higher experimental concentrations affected growth and developmental scores. This is a reason for further investigation and caution, but it does not measure the risk after a person drinks a commercial tea or takes a capsule. Direct embryo exposure, isolated chemicals and animal development differ from an oral human exposure.

A 2008 review discussed a reassuring human cohort alongside laboratory concerns, noting the high experimental concentrations and limited evidence. Its conclusion was still cautious, especially in early pregnancy. A small or reassuring observation cannot establish safety, while a concerning laboratory result cannot prove that a particular pregnancy has been harmed. No reliable individual risk percentage or safe serving can be calculated from these findings.

Breastfeeding has its own unanswered questions

The LactMed ginseng entry, last revised in December 2021 and checked for this article, identifies no published measurements of maternal or infant levels and no adequate information about effects on breastfed infants or milk production. It notes that many sources advise avoiding ginseng while nursing because of limited evidence and possible estrogen-like activity. That concern is not a measurement of what reaches a baby.

Do not take ginseng to increase milk supply. If you have already used it, ask a pharmacist or breastfeeding clinician about the specific product, amount, timing and your baby’s circumstances. The available evidence cannot supply a dependable waiting interval or a blanket instruction to discard milk. Obtain an individual feeding plan rather than stopping breastfeeding solely because of this article.

Side effects and interactions deserve attention

Reported adverse effects include insomnia, digestive upset, headache, rash and, in some reports, blood-pressure changes or vaginal bleeding. A reported event is not proof that every preparation causes it. Health Canada advises stopping the product and seeking advice if insomnia, anxiety or headaches occur. Unexpected symptoms should be assessed rather than automatically attributed to ginseng. If you are pregnant and have any vaginal bleeding or spotting, contact maternity or early-pregnancy care urgently, even without pain. Heavy bleeding, or bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, faintness or collapse, needs emergency care now. Use your local emergency number; do not assume the bleeding is just a supplement side effect.

Show the full medicine and supplement list to a pharmacist. Health Canada specifically flags diabetes, antidepressants, blood thinners and digoxin for advice before use. Ginseng may affect blood sugar, and NCCIH also raises concerns about clotting and autoimmune conditions. Evidence for particular interactions varies; do not change prescribed medicines yourself to accommodate a supplement.

Check teas, drinks and supplement labels

Look beyond the front-label promise of energy or wellness. Check for ginseng in herbal blends, energy products, smoothie additives and other drinks, and record the botanical name, extract strength, amount per serving and all additional ingredients. Being sold as a beverage does not establish that an ingredient is appropriate in pregnancy. An unspecified blend also makes exposure harder to assess.

This does not mean that every herbal tea is dangerous. MotherToBaby distinguishes moderate culinary use of herbs from medicinal preparations and stresses that products differ. Some herbs can affect hormones or uterine activity; that is not evidence that all teas cause miscarriage. Ask about the actual ingredients rather than replacing ginseng with another unreviewed blend.

Natural, regulated and safe are different questions

In the United States, the FDA does not approve dietary supplements for safety and effectiveness before sale. That is not the same as saying supplements are entirely unregulated, or that every herbal food is a drug. Regulatory systems elsewhere differ. A registration, traditional-use claim or quality seal does not by itself establish pregnancy or breastfeeding safety.

Herbal preparations can vary in concentration and may contain contaminants or ingredients not listed accurately. Liquid preparations can also contain alcohol. Bring the actual packaging, or clear photographs of every label panel, to the consultation; the brand name alone may be insufficient.

What if you have already taken ginseng?

Do not take further nonprescribed medicinal ginseng while arranging advice. Write down the exact product, how much you used, how often, when you last took it, your stage of pregnancy or your baby’s age, and any symptoms. Include other medicines and supplements. These details let the clinician assess an actual exposure rather than the word ginseng in isolation.

A prior exposure is not a diagnosis of fetal or infant harm. Ask whether anything beyond your usual care is appropriate; do not assume that extra testing, a change to prescribed treatment or interruption of breastfeeding is automatically necessary. If the product was recommended by a clinician, contact that clinician to review the reason for use and available alternatives.

If fatigue is why you were considering it

Tiredness is common in pregnancy, particularly early on. NHS guidance emphasizes rest, help from others, a healthy diet and suitable activity. A walk or other comfortable activity may help, while evening caffeine can make sleep harder. Practical support is often more useful than adding another product to an already complicated routine.

Tell your maternity team when tiredness or poor sleep is difficult to manage. If sleeplessness comes with hopelessness or loss of interest in things you usually enjoy, seek help from your doctor or midwife. The aim is to understand what you need, rather than assume an energy supplement will solve the problem.

When a reaction needs urgent help

Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, collapse or marked confusion after a product can signal a severe allergic reaction. Call your local emergency number immediately. If you have a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector, use it as instructed; do not wait for a routine supplement consultation.

For other suspected adverse effects, stop the supplement and seek medical advice. Keep the packaging so the product can be identified. Reporting a suspected reaction through your local medicine or supplement safety system can also help identify product problems.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current official guidance supports caution because pregnancy and breastfeeding evidence is inadequate; traditional use does not establish safety.

The 2003 embryo experiment and 2008 review are historical context. Their findings cannot determine an individual exposure risk.

Product identity, preparation, medicines and the reason for use all matter when discussing a personal decision.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize questions about a product and record its label, timing and symptoms. It cannot approve a supplement, determine fetal or infant risk, or replace your clinician or pharmacist.

When to seek help

This is educational information, not an individual treatment or feeding plan. Seek emergency care for signs of a severe allergic reaction. In pregnancy, obtain urgent maternity advice for any bleeding or spotting; heavy bleeding or bleeding with severe abdominal or shoulder pain, faintness or collapse needs emergency care now. Obtain professional advice about ginseng use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Avoid using medicinal ginseng on your own during pregnancy or breastfeeding; arrange a review of the exact product.
  • Panax ginseng, American ginseng and Siberian ginseng should not be treated as interchangeable.
  • Laboratory findings justify caution but cannot predict the outcome of an individual exposure.
  • Check mixed drinks and herbal blends, as well as capsules, and disclose other medicines.
  • If you already used ginseng, record the details and seek tailored advice without assuming harm.

Frequently asked questions

Is ginseng safe to take during pregnancy?

Safety has not been established, and no pregnancy-safe dose can be recommended from the evidence reviewed here. Avoid self-treatment and ask your maternity clinician or pharmacist about the exact preparation. Later pregnancy should not be treated as an automatically safe window.

What benefits does ginseng have?

Some studies in nonpregnant adults suggest limited benefits for particular outcomes, but findings are often small or inconsistent. These results do not establish a treatment for pregnancy fatigue, a benefit for fetal development or protection against cancer. Match each claim to the population and outcome actually studied.

What side effects can oral ginseng cause?

Reported effects include trouble sleeping, headache, digestive symptoms and skin reactions. Medicine interactions also matter. Stop the supplement and seek advice for a suspected reaction; breathing difficulty, sudden throat swelling or collapse needs emergency care.

Can I take ginseng while breastfeeding?

Avoid unsupervised use. Reliable information about milk transfer and effects on infants is lacking. If you have already taken it, seek product-specific advice; there is no established waiting interval that this article can safely offer.

Is ginseng tea safer than a capsule?

The form alone cannot establish safety. Species, concentration, quantity and other ingredients differ. Take the tea packaging to your pharmacist rather than assuming a drink is harmless or that all herbal teas are unsafe.

Does one accidental exposure mean my baby was harmed?

No such conclusion can be drawn from exposure alone. Record the product, amount and timing and contact your care team for an individual assessment. Animal experiments do not provide a reliable risk estimate for your situation.

What about a cream containing ginseng?

Evidence about oral use cannot simply be applied to a skin product. NCCIH says there is insufficient information about the safety of topical Asian ginseng, which can irritate skin. Ask about the exact formulation and intended application, especially if a breastfeeding baby could contact the treated area.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
